sm: Host Kyle Peterson and his Wall Street Journal colleagues Joe Sternberg and Zach Kessel discuss the fallout from Tuesday's midterms, with Democrats at 253 House seats and 54 Senate seats, not counting Alaska and Mississippi, where they lead. President Trump announced that Stephen Miller will become chief of staff on Monday, while Susie Wiles moves to his political operation. Sternberg notes Wiles had health issues and might have left anyway, but says the bigger problem is that Miller architected the aggressive immigration roundups that put off voters. Kessel adds that Miller reportedly pushed detention quotas for ICE, and says Trump may now govern in a more maximalist way, largely through executive orders. On the markets, Sternberg says questions about an AI investment bubble were already building, and Democratic wins at the state level, including in Texas, raise worries about state regulation of AI and data centers.

Sternberg says the day's jobs report was strong and broad-based, no longer concentrated in healthcare, but it looks backward, while markets worry about the AI story and new political changes. The panel then turns to the Senate and the courts. Republicans could confirm judges in the lame duck, and Chuck Schumer told the Associated Press that Democrats will not allow a right-winger on the Supreme Court. Kessel points out that Justice Alito is seventy-six and Justice Thomas seventy-eight, and that Republicans may not win the Senate back until 2032, or even 2034, according to Peterson. They review the 2028 map, including Republican seats in North Carolina, Wisconsin, Iowa and Alaska, and Democratic questions in Pennsylvania, Arizona and Georgia. Sternberg urges against despair, saying the electorate is volatile and both parties overreach after winning, though incumbency will help Democrats.

Kessel says Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff, who won by almost twenty points, is getting talk as a 2028 Democratic nominee. He argues Ossoff's record on Israel, including a vote against some arms packages after October seventh, helps him in a primary. The panel then plays Ron DeSantis saying no one in the party has Trump's outsized brand, so it must be ideas based. Sternberg agrees that a party built on one personality is volatile, and Kessel says ideas could cut the chaos voters disliked. Kessel warns Democrats about Abdul El-Sayed's Medicare for All push, noting ballot measures in Iowa, North Carolina and Ohio went in conservative directions on taxes and voter ID. He cites a Third Way analysis that progressive candidates in Michigan, Minnesota and Maine ran about five points behind their party's statewide vote. Sternberg expects the activist base to over-interpret the results and push for a progressive in 2028.
